Definition: Workflow specificity: There should only be a single pipeline per data or analysis type.
Workflow name: Names should be lower case and without punctuation.
Use the template: All pipelines must be built using the nf-core template and pipeline initialization with nf-core pipelines create (nf-core/tools version 3.3.2).
Remove nf-core branding by selecting 'Custom' during workflow creation in the nf-core pipelines create UI.
Docker support: Software must be bundled using Docker and versioned.

Semantic versioning: Pipelines must use stable release tags following MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format (e.g., 2.1.0), where MAJOR indicates breaking changes, MINOR indicates backward-compatible feature additions, and PATCH indicates backward-compatible bug fixes.
Use consistent parameter naming conventions and CLI options across workflows, following established project standards where applicable.
Minimum inputs: Pipelines should be able to run with as little input as possible.
Use nf-core git branches: Use master, dev, and TEMPLATE. Naming convention main is allowable for master.
Presence of directories as applicable: assets, bin, conf, docs, modules, subworkflows, workflows.
Modules/containers must utilize actively maintained software and tool versions and avoid deprecated/old packages to ensure long-term viability.
Inputs and outputs are properly channelized and atomized (i.e., individual files are passed, not directories).
References to the repository name and GitHub organization should be consistent throughout the repository.
Publication credit: Pipeline publications should acknowledge the nf-core community.
All public health pipelines should be identified as part of the ph-core namespace in the README.
Continuous integration testing: Pipelines must run CI tests in GitHub Actions.
Pass lint tests: The pipeline must not have any undocumented failures in the nf-core lint tests. A failure is documented when it is disabled in the lint section of .nf-core.yml.
Testing: Use nf-test to test that the pipeline completes successfully with valid outputs using a minimal example (see https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VaKcd_qgBJc).
The nf-core linting step must run as part of GitHub Actions CI.

Use the nf-core tools CLI (nf-core/tools) to keep pipeline versioning and nf-core template-derived configuration files synced and validated (e.g., bump-version, lint, schema build), rather than editing them manually.
Index referencing should use column names instead of positional indexing.
Presence of subworkflows directory when subworkflows are needed.
Module containers must reference a specific container version (not 'latest').
Only one process defined within each individual module (see https://nf-co.re/events/2021/bytesize-5-dsl2-module-development).
For meta fields, using the standard meta.id or meta.single_end is encouraged. Non-standard fields can be used, but they should be documented with justifications in the checklist Notes column.

Each module must emit a versions.yml file containing the version number for each tool, without a leading "v" (e.g., 1.2.3, not v1.2.3). For software unable to output version number, enter it manually. For unversioned software, use Git SHA commit ID.
Modules should be stored in the modules directory, and local modules should follow the same directory structure and naming conventions as nf-core modules.
Parse tabular data with Nextflow operators (e.g., metadata handling with collectFile) where possible. Use safe and robust indexing (e.g., by field name) within bin scripts.
Testing data for custom modules should be accessible (e.g., in nf-core/test-datasets or the organization's test data repository).

Place scripts in bin/ with a portable shebang (e.g., #!/usr/bin/env python3) and executable permissions, and have modules call them by name (e.g., summarize_coverage.py ..., not python3 summarize_coverage.py ...).

Use multithreading or parallelization to reduce bottlenecks in computationally or memory-intensive processes, while respecting allocated resources (i.e., the CPUs/memory assigned to the task by Nextflow).

Keep script logic clear: avoid unnecessary nesting to improve readability, and cache/reuse computed values or parsed data structures instead of recomputing or reparsing them to reduce potential bugs and redundant processing.

Custom scripts in bin/ that implement their own multithreading or multiprocessing must derive the worker/thread count from the CPUs allocated by Nextflow (e.g., $task.cpus passed in as an environment variable or argument), rather than querying the host's CPU count (e.g., Python's os.cpu_count()).

Avoid legacy or inefficient data structures (e.g., plain arrays with repeated linear scans) in scripts and modules; prefer Nextflow channels or keyed lookups (e.g., maps/dictionaries) where appropriate for performance and clarity.
